utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we go into private session for a few matters, perhaps the first thing in relation to scheduling is that I was informed, Mr. Krajisnik, that you have a dentist appointment this Thursday - is that correct? - between 8.00 and 9.00?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I said that it should be this week, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm informed that it would be this Thursday, and so therefore Thursday is already a bit deviant from our usual days, but that would then sit -- start at a late start. I take it, I hope, at 9.30 we could start, then we will most likely finish at approximately 11.00 and have a longer break, and then have a session until 3.00 or 3.30. So that's the first scheduling issue. Then I would like to turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Krajisnik, today again we received a short list of material from you. We have dealt with it in the same way that it's given to the parties. They can use it and introduce it into evidence if they think that it would assist them. At the same time, at the end of your testimony any documentation which is not adopted, so to say, by the parties, you will have an opportunity to explain on the basis of the then-translated inventories, as you know the inventories were the first ones to be translated, to apply for admission into evidence of specific documents and explain to the Chamber why you consider them of importance for the Chamber. Then at the very end of your testimony, we'll also go through the list of exhibits that have been introduced through you as a witness. We'll then hear -- we'll review the material. We'll hear objections to the evidence which was introduced. Mr. Registrar is invited to prepare that list so that the parties could prepare properly and that we do not spend too much time on that evidence and the admission of that evidence and that I can make short reference to the numbers on the list. Then a very practical matter. I do understand that when I gave, on behalf of the Chamber, the deadline for objections in relation to the photographic material, Mr. Krajisnik, the deadline was addressed to you, that the transcript now reads that it was one week after the 21st of June, whereas from what I understood that's not what I said. You have up until tomorrow to come up with any objections in relation to that photographic material. And I already instructed you what kind of objections the Chamber would expect. Then another very practical matter is the following. It's quite some time ago that there was an objection by the Defence to the admission into evidence of the notebook of Mr. Karadzic. And at that time it was uncertain on what other portions of that same notebook would be raised during the examination of witnesses by the OTP. Therefore, we delayed at that time a decision on whether the whole of the notebook would be admitted or whether the Chamber would follow the objection by the Defence, that is only to admit those portions that were specifically dealt with during the examination of the witness. We are now further on in the case. I do not remember that the notebook of Mr. Karadzic returned since that date, so the OTP is invited to reconsider its position as far as admission of the totality or just part of the notebook of Mr. Karadzic is concerned, to express itself on the matter so that we can hear from the Defence what their position is. Then finally, and that is a procedurally bit complicated matter. A letter has been sent by Mr. Karadzic to the Defence. That letter has been translated. I take it that the parties received the translation. The letter was introduced by Mr. Krajisnik as a witness. It is not clear to the Chamber whether any of the parties would adopt that letter to -- in the sense that they would tender it into evidence or whether they would not. If they do not, then it still is a document which was in the hands of a witness who presented it to the Chamber, and the Chamber would - so therefore, if it's not adopted by any of the parties - would like to hear whether there are any objections to admit this letter as a -- as an exhibit brought by a witness during his examination as a witness. And there I do understand that the position of the Defence is a bit complicated because you are in a position to express a position as Defence counsel of the accused in relation to a document which has been brought to the attention of the Chamber by a witness who happens to be the accused as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm happy to say that we can at least make it simpler in this respect. Two points: We don't adopt it, but we don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear. Any position already from the Defence -- from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, but we'll get one back to the Court very quickly, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And of course an admission into evidence is apart from weight to be given, how to evaluate the material, the level of relevance, that's of course a matter which is apart from admission as such. Having dealt with these practical matters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that CLSS would like to check the translation of a document which the Defence expected to receive today, and that would then be early tomorrow and same would be true for the OTP. Yes. Then having dealt with these practical and procedural matters, Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like to remind you that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau reminds me that there was a tiny thing, Mr. Stewart, you would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's very gracious of him to remember that and to note it. Yes, I did. Yes, it was this -- Your Honour, it was only looking ahead in the light of that timetable. We -- of course we have Your Honours' questions now, Your Honours in the plural, is there -- may we have a -- is there some indication -- do Your Honours have in mind a point at which Your Honours will have completed your questions and there will be the opportunity for the parties? Because I have it in mind also the apparent slight uncertainty about the position in relation to next Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I simply say -- Your Honour would appreciate, the Trial Chamber and the parties don't always see a hundred per cent eye to eye about the scale of the demands on the case, but at the very least this is going to be a pretty demanding period for both parties. The more we can know about where we're going -- and I rather feel that Mr. Harmon is sharing my submission on this, Your Honour - the better for all concerned. He apparently clearly does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, if that's more helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony. And before I give an opportunity to Judge Hanoteau to continue to put questions to you, I have one simple question on the documents you provided to us today. There's one handwritten document on which I clearly see the name of Mr. Silajdzic appear. Could you briefly tell us what the document approximately is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave evidence yesterday in response to a question to a question by Judge Hanoteau concerning a girl that I brought to the airport, and that is what the document is about. I didn't want to mention either his or her name, especially not her name. I typed it out on the second page, the exact same thing that I provided in manuscript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then can -- who was Mr. Silajdzic exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Silajdzic was a member of the negotiating team on the Muslim side. He was the foreign minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina and also Prime Minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, yesterday when adjourned we had mentioned the presence of Mr. Davidovic on the territory of your country, and I asked whether at one point in time you felt that around you things were hidden from you. And you answered that you hadn't felt that and that you couldn't even imagine that people were hiding information from you. So in your answer I thought I understood that you were reducing that to the presence of Mr. Davidovic on the territory, but my question was a bit broader. I wanted to know whether you felt that the information was hidden from you on the weapons that were equipping the Serbs, on the problem of the role paramilitaries were playing. You know that in this Tribunal you know we've heard a lot of evidence on this, and often you told us: Well, I didn't know, I didn't know. So here's my question: Have you ever felt that around you people were hiding information from you, but deliberately because people didn't want you to know about this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for asking that question again because I don't think I've managed to give a complete and good answer. When I responded to your question I said that I didn't have the impression that people in my immediate as I recall with whom I cooperated, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, Mrs. Plavsic, people from the authorities with whom I had contact, were keeping things from me at those consultative meetings. However, each of us was busy doing his or her own job in an autonomous way, just like the government is not aware of what I was doing, I was not aware what the government was doing. It's similar with members of the Presidency. There are many decisions of the Presidency - I'm not saying that they are criminal - but that I was not aware of until seeing them here because it was up to the authority concerned to issue such decisions. As for paramilitary units, it was said here that the SDS, the Serb Democratic Party, was involved in the distribution of weapons. That point was made here several times. I really had nothing to do with that line of party work, and I was not really informed whether somebody was shipping weapons by trailer from some other area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As for paramilitary units, I assure you that it was the firm position of the army and also of the people with whom I had those consultative meetings that that was an evil and that they had to be placed under the control of the army, because otherwise there would be no control. Because the army was badly organised as it was. It consisted basically of armed citizens. And it was my sincere belief that everybody concerned was committed to fighting against paramilitary units. As for Pale and the leadership in Pale, I would be hard-put to say whether somebody was concealing a group of, let's say, 20 men that I didn't know about. But it's very hard to say because we were short of man-power and municipalities wanted to fill those empty trenches, and maybe on their own initiative they sought help elsewhere. However, that was forbidden, and if that was done it could only have been done by the lower level, on their own initiative, without the consent or the knowledge of the government. As for the government and the Presidency, I don't think they were keeping things from me; they were just doing their job, although there were a lot of things that came within their province that I didn't know about until now. For instance, that law that we discussed earlier. It was drafted, it was given to the president of the Presidency to sign, and that was the procedure that completely bypassed me because it was not my job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And along the same line of thought, Mr. Krajisnik, let's go back to the report that was drafted by the Sarajevo MUP and that dealt with a police action that arrested a vehicle that was loaded with automatic weapons, with a lot of ammunition. It was a vehicle where a Mr. Kostic Dusan was, a person who was a member of the SDS Main Board, Mr. -- and he was an MP, Mr. Kostic Dusan. So you said that you never heard about this report that had been drafted by the Sarajevo MUP. So here's my comment, and there's a question after it. When a police department, police service, is in this delicate situation like we have right here - there is the police that is in front of an MP, and I mean they're very close to an offence here. So you could think that the people in charge at the police department - you know, for the ministry - would immediately alert the person in charge of the institution that this person belongs to. So I would like to get an explanation from you. I'd like you to tell us how you could imagine that the minister of the home interior, learning this and being so surprised, didn't report to you, you as president of the Assembly. I mean, you were the boss of the MPs, after all, if I could say so, the "boss." Do you think that this -- the minister of interior wanted to hide the reality from you? And that was what I was talking about earlier, the deliberate will to hide things from you. Or do you think there were other intents behind all this? How do you feel about all this? Because the reality is there, it exists.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, at that time the MUP was a joint institution of Bosnia and Herzegovina and a Muslim man was at its head. Now, from this distance, with hindsight, I can give you my opinion but that's probably not what you're interested in. You're probably interested in what I thought then. There was this story that the MUP was arming Muslims, that a reserve police force was being established, etc. There were a lot of irregularities and Parliament was never officially informed, instead there was backroom talk, you know when... before the session, why it never... What was the MUP Minister supposed to do? He should have presented it to the Government, the Government presents to the Assembly the official information, files a criminal report and it goes to the Public Prosecutor’s Office and that Office takes its own course. According to our Constitution, the Speaker of the Assembly has no authority over the conduct of MPs, the Assembly does. The Assembly itself does have that control. They can strip an MP of his immunity and deprive him of other sorts of protection. However, it was a time when there was no real authority in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and these illegal factions, they tolerated each other, knowing that the other one was also distributing weapons. I have no other explanation for why no measures were undertaken at the time to... there is a way for doing things, no need to reinvent the wheel... Regardless of whether it was an MP, or anyone else, things take their course as they should...and whoever ambushed the convoy and everything else. So he did not have to report to me personally. He should have informed the Government, the Government in turn should have informed the Assembly; he could have reported it to me but he didn’t have to, he was under no obligation to do so or to say we demand that immunity be stripped or that the issue be debated. So, that was the established route, unfortunately we kept blaming one another and so you could never tell what was truth and what was rumour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you another question, Mr. Krajisnik, regarding another topic. At the Assembly session held on the 25th of February, 2005 [as interpreted], you stated the following, and I will quote you in English. You stated: [In English] "We have two options: One to fight by political means, to make the most out of the present time as a first phase; or to break off the talks and go for what we have done over the centuries, win our own territories by force." [Interpretation] A little further down you stated: [In English] "-- remain in a single Serbia, with Serbia and Montenegro," and so on. "If we don't want to do this by certain methods, let us put a stop to it. You know what our provision has always been, to wage war." [Interpretation] You recall, Mr. Krajisnik, saying this, do you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I don't recall which session it was, but I remember my words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It certainly would not have been in 2005, as the transcript reads, but please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, it was the 25th of February, 1992. Mr. Krajisnik, my question was the following. In the statement you are not saying that the use of force will be applied only if you are attacked, but you are considering using force as of the moment where the political negotiations do not work out. You say in your statement: If the negotiations are not fruitful, we are going to wage a war. What did you mean by that, exactly, or is this what you meant? You are not alluding to an imminent aggression which would justify the use of offensive or the use of force. We feel, when we re-read your statement, that in case of the negotiations -- in case they don't work out, you will take this initiative to wage a war. Should I understand you like this or maybe did I perhaps misunderstand you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will tell you what my thinking was and what things were in reality, and it's up to you to judge that. What was on the agenda was an agreement - you can look it up at that Assembly session - an agreement from the conference that was to be discussed by the MPs. MPs had a thousand objections. They were bothered by this and that, whereas the Muslims had already declared their referendum and going for independence. So you had many MPs saying: What's the use of talking to them anyway? Because they are going for their referendum and they are going to vote for an independent Bosnia without any transformation. So the point was to persuade these people who were bitter about being led up the garden path for a whole year, as they were saying, and to persuade them that we should continue with negotiations. So I said we had -- we have two options: To find a solution through negotiations. And then sarcastically I say: We have option number two. Just as we waged war for years, losing lives, getting killed, we can do that now, without having exhausted the possibilities of option one. And you will see from the transcript of that session that it was with great difficulty that we forced the Assembly to approve the continued negotiations, because they were up in arms saying: The Muslims are going for independence irrespective of the constitution, irrespective of anything. And I wanted to tell you this: I understood the role of the Speaker of the Assembly in the following way. I thought that it was my obligation to make sure that the conclusions and decisions were correct, legal, and regular. And whatever contributions, whatever speeches by MPs that were maybe immoderate and whatever it took to continue the deliberations was a small price to pay for ultimately reaching a decision. And I analysed the decisions taken by that Assembly, and I did not find a single one that I would like now to dissociate myself from. Not a single decision was illegal. For instance, if an MP rose and said: Let's vote for option two, war, I never put such a decision up for a vote. I never allowed a single decision to be taken under the influence of somebody's passions. I only cared for the result, and that was the most important thing for me. Because Serbs had gone through many wars. Each of those wars halved their population. There could have been without wars 30 million Serbs instead of today's 7 or 8 million. The point of my speech was not advocating war; on the contrary. If you analyse it, you will see that it was all a commitment to peace and negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Changing topic to ask you the following question. Mr. Stewart quoted Mr. Karadzic and he quoted certain things. He said, pertaining to the power, how to take power, so he is quoting and is criticising little Napoleons who are trying to hurt or who are doing things that will inevitably do the Serbian people wrong. When asked to give your opinion on that quote from Karadzic you answered: [In English] "People of the regional level got to be in charge of the region SDS policies and grabbed power, elevated themselves, and decided they were independent of the party." [Interpretation] And later on you added. [In English] " -- Mr. Karadzic put some people on the regional level in charge of coordinating regional boards of the SDS so these people acquired a certain power and, to put it crudely, they abused it." [Interpretation] You did not want to give names, you did not want to mention people whom you thought said that. You said it would be just guesswork, you did not want it to go into detail. You thought that we would definitely understand, but what did you mean when you said: These people in fact had abused power, had -- when you said that these small Napoleons, these people who abused power, what did you mean exactly, who did you have in mind exactly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was precisely this example when Mr. Karadzic used those words, he was criticising one of the presidents, one of the regional coordinators for SDS from Banja Luka. He is a wonderful man, but he is very stubborn, not disciplined at all. And the policy of the SDS, meanwhile, and our policy was to observe the Vance Plan in Croatia and to work for the transformation of Bosnia and Herzegovina according to Cutileiro principles. We couldn't split Croatia and split Bosnia and tear them apart because that would be a blow to international agreements. However, bowing to the great wish of the Krajina people from the Serbian Krajina and the Bosnian Krajina, those people wanted to proclaim Krajinas a state. We were aware that the Krajina people wanted it; however, we had to tell them: No. No because of this reason and that reason. That particular man was heading this initiative and making such statements, and then people from the international community rightfully said: You are not observing international agreements and how can we trust you in our negotiations if you are obviously trying to split up Bosnia and Croatia? That man in that job was under obligation to tell the Krajina people what they didn't necessarily like to hear, namely that they had certainly obligations, they couldn't just do as they pleased. And whatever action they took would have certain consequences. Another thing. Economic power lay with municipalities because they had a certain income and revenues. They financed the army, the refugees, and the fact is that political power is always coupled with economic power. And in wartime when all ties are severed, it's difficult to synchronise things. If you do not have any carrots to offer, those people on that level will do as they please. I'm not saying that everybody was like that. Those people like him were exceptions. Most people behaved quite decently. But those few exceptions were enough to create trouble. That is the example that I remember when I hear those words of Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, I would like to quote you again. It is something that you said on the 18th of March, 1992. It is something you uttered during the 18th Assembly Session. You stated the following. [In English] "I think the problem is that they want BH to be internationally recognised at any cost. They want it to be a state. In this respect it would be good if we could do one thing for strategic reasons, if we could start implementing that we have agreed upon the ethnic division on the ground, that we start determining the territory, and once the territory is determined it remains to be established in additional negotiations whose authorities are to function and in what way." [Interpretation] And you concluded by saying. [In English] "I can't say whether we'll be fair in political terms. There is no much fairness in politics after all, and if it doesn't turn out to be fair, the Serbian will be blamed." [Interpretation] You may recall your words. You may recall what you said at that time.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you said: "We could start implementing that which we had agreed upon, the ethnic division on the ground, we have to start determining the territory," by that did you mean that it -- does this involve a taking of a territory according to an ethnic line or an ethnic division that was already decided upon earlier? Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Cutileiro principles were on the agenda and I state quite clearly -- well, perhaps what is written there is ambiguous. Let us carry out what we have agreed on. I meant the principles, namely that we should know what our ethnic areas are. There was a map there, and what the ethnic areas were. Through negotiations we will try to get as much as possible, at any rate I wanted to get even more territory because this was say 44 per cent or whatever. As for government and whose government would function where, it depended on whether it would be the constituent unit or Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was said it would be the Bosnia and Herzegovina government and the government of the constituent unit. I know that this sounds equivocal, but if you analyse that Assembly people invariably wanted to go back to the option of Yugoslavia. So that was a turning point for us to say: Well, this is Bosnia -- well, I couldn't put it in those words. But let us carry through what we've agreed upon and then let's try to achieve as much as possible through talks. It took a lot of time for people to move from one concept to another, namely from remaining in Yugoslavia together with all the other Serbs to a Bosnia where they would have their own constituent unit. You will see in the debate that people said: What is this constituent unit? They will do this, they will do that to us. A plan that was similar on the 11th of March went down the drain, and then it was adopted through a major effort. That was my objective. Of course my objective was not war if we were talking about the Cutileiro principles. For me what was important was that we know that we have in Krajina, Herzegovina, Semberija, what we have agreed upon, these are our areas, but everybody would want his village to be in the constituent unit or his own region, and then you say: Wait a second, we'll negotiate -- oh, I'm sorry, I got carried away. I'm moving very fast. When the MPs were debating things, it was only maps that were a problem, territories were the only problem. Everybody was just trying to see on which side his own home area would be. Would it be green or blue or red? And we say: Let us carry through what we've agreed upon, and then we'll go on talking and we'll see what kind of government there will be on the whole and what kind of government there will be in the constituent unit. That was the only point of my discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there, Mr. Krajisnik, I will tell you a bit what is puzzling me in the statement is that when -- what you said in conclusion: "I cannot say whether this will be fair in political terms," this seems to mean that what I'm saying here is try to determine these territories. I know that it's not very, very pretty, but that's what politics are. So that comment that you add at the end in fact makes the beginning of your statement completely ambiguous. Do you see yourself that one could understand your words that way or how should we understand it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully understand that this can be understood in different ways. We always had a club meeting before the Assembly, and the atmosphere there was always more relaxed. I know that we were saying: Look at this. We are 33 per cent and the Cutileiro Plan gives us 44 per cent. We wanted to sell that plan, so to speak. And when we said we will go on striving for territories, well perhaps it's not going to be fair for us to get, I don't know, 50 per cent. What I was trying to tell them was that what will be achieved in addition to all of this is perhaps not all that fair because our percentage of the population is less. Well, I have to say that in order to sell the plan so that the people would adopt it. You know, sometimes you say something that you yourself know is not correct, that is to say you have 64 per cent of the territory. And then you say: Wait a second. You look at the arguments of the Muslims and they say: Wait a second, there is only 33 per cent of you and you're getting 44 per cent of the territory. That's what I'm saying. So if through negotiations we get a bit more and that's unfair, that's politics. I wanted them to realise that they should be satisfied with what we are getting now as a point of departure, so to speak, rather than have megalomaniac aspirations. Somebody would like to take, I don't know, two-thirds of Bosnia, or whatever. It depends on how people viewed the division of Bosnia. I'm so sorry. You can see that at club meetings the atmosphere was far more relaxed than at the session, but then some things only continued at the session itself. I always wanted a fair settlement, always. And when we talked to the other two sides as well I always said that I didn't want something to work to the advantage of the Serb people and to the disadvantage of the other two peoples. The Serbs really had a lot of territory, truth to tell all of that are unproductive areas that were not exactly built-up. But that is a fact. And we got these unproductive parts. We did not get the developed parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, I would like you to elaborate on one last point. If I understood correctly you were elected by the Main Board of the SDS on the 12th of July, 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly of the Serb Democratic Party; yes, the 12th of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And at that time you were a member of the SDS for how long?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the SDS from the very outset, that is to say from the 12th of July, 1990. I was a member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So I am not mistaken in saying that you were not part of the Executive Board of the SDS. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not in the Main Board or the Executive Board until the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I see. So the Main Board was comprised of 45 members, if I understood you correctly. Is that exact? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Executive Board was comprised of how many members?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was six, seven, eight, or nine, that's a smaller body, as a government is in the republic. It's sort of an executive body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please give me an idea of the -- the number of meetings of the Main Board, what was the frequency of your meetings, how often did you meet, as of the 12th of July, 1991? As of the moment when you began to participate. Those meetings took place at what frequency? How often would you meet?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was here that I established how many session had been held. In actual fact I think there were two or three sessions before the war broke out. I think that there were several joint sessions of the members of the Main Board and the Club of Deputies when an important problem was supposed to be resolved. According to the records or minutes, I think there is one or two sessions of the Main Board. There is also this telephone conversation between Mr. Dukic and myself towards the end of the year when he says that the Main Board had not met for almost a year. Indeed, the Main Board was not operating. It was this joint Assembly that was focussed upon in perhaps these joint meetings. So the work of the Main Board was not really felt. Operative work carried by the Executive Board of the Serb Democratic Party was in the forefront.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that what you meant when you talked about the SDS Political Council, that council?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour. There was a separate body consisting of prominent individuals, members of the academy, and so on. It was an advisory body. I was not a member of the Political Council, but I am aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So this Executive Board, if I understood you correctly, met two or three times before the beginning of the war. Is that correct? And after that, there were no meetings and the club -- the Deputies' Club was the instance where one would discuss politics. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The Executive Board met frequently, that executive body that I was not a member of. The Main Board had only two or three sessions. So what was the policy? Unfortunately only one question. The policy was discussing the fate of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At these joint meetings that is what was discussed, if that was the subject involved. Other matters, personnel movements and so on, were resolved by the executive body. I did not attend any meetings of the Executive Board, due to my own commitments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Now I'd like to know how this Deputies' Club operated. You know, it's mentioned often, so how did it work? This Deputies' Club existed within the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So was it a Deputies' Club with only SDS members?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and two MPs of the SPO, that's the party of Vuk Draskovic. In Bosnia-Herzegovina that's the way it was, yes. Later on there were independent MPs as well in the Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. But at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina - we'll stay there for now - this Deputies' Club brought together the deputies that were SDS and two others that were of another party. But at the time, what was the role played by this Deputies' Club? Did they have a legal existence? Was it something that was provided for in the constitution? And then secondly, what role did it play? But only for Bosnia-Herzegovina right now.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. According to the rules of procedure of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, every political party that had its deputies in the Assembly, if it had at least two deputies it had the right to establish its own club. There were three political parties -- or rather, two political parties that had two members respectively. They had their own rooms, they had their own secretary that the Assembly gave them. The club -- or rather, all clubs met when they would get materials for Assembly meetings. Then before the Assembly meeting they would meet and prepare for the session that was to be held the following day. This material would be elaborated on in preparation for the following day. There were also ad hoc meetings of the club during breaks if there was a problem, and then the clubs would withdraw and discuss a particular matter. The president of the club had an office of his own. There was the secretary of the club, too, and there was an official representative of the Assembly there from the administration who helped him in his work. This was an official body. Every political party in the Assembly had that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. But at the time of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who was chairing the Deputies' Club, the SDS Deputies' Club, who was chairing it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a president and a deputy president of the club. The president of the club was Professor Vojislav Maksimovic and the deputy president was Trifko Radic, MP. They chaired the meetings of the Deputies' Club, they gave the floor to others, they took part in the discussion themselves, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you were president of the Assembly and you also sat at the Deputies' Club, right.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when Republika Srpska was created there was a new Assembly, and there again was there also a Deputies' Club?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The same two people were the president and the deputy president, and all of us were the Deputies' Club, including the independent MPs. At first they were together with us and later on they had a separate club of their own, that is to say towards the end. Pretty late, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this Assembly of Republika Srpska, if I understood things well, there were no new elections to elect the MPs of Republika Srpska. It's the SDS MPs -- well, it's the Serbian deputies of the Bosnian Assembly who became the MPs of the Assembly of Republika Srpska. Is that the way it worked?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Serbs who were deputies in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not only from the SDS but also from other parties, they became the Serb Assembly, only those MPs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in this Assembly of Republika Srpska, were there several Deputies' Club or just one Deputies' Club?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first there was just one, one club. We were all a club. And later on -- well, maybe in 1994 and 1995, I can't say exactly, the MPs from other parties established their own club.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in this Assembly of Republika Srpska, this Deputies' Club, did it meet every day? Could you tell me exactly how often the Deputies' Club met?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It only met when an Assembly session was supposed to be held. The club did not meet apart from Assembly sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you did not chair this Deputies' Club, right? Mr. Maksimovic was still chairing this Deputies' Club?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Maksimovic and Radic again, the two of them were still president and deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understood you well, Mr. Krajisnik, during those meetings of the Deputies' Club in Republika Srpska, there were also people who were not members -- MPs who attended, right? I didn't think that I made a mistake, but I think I understood that Mr. Karadzic sometimes attended, members of the government, ministers, even General Mladic attended?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'm afraid -- I'm sorry to say that you're mixing this hodgepodge, you know, it's a bit strange. I mean, a Deputies' Club would be a place normally where people would be thinking, you know? Where MPs would be thinking about the decisions that they're about to make in a session. But why is there such a mix-up? You know, because here is a body where you're supposed to be thinking and drafting, but you also have people who are in government who are attending. I mean, I don't have anything against military, of course, but you also have people from military come and attend. So how can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that the military were there only if there would be a session and then a break. If club meetings were held before the session, I do not recall that the members of the military were ever present. If they would come to a session and then if the club would meet -- well, I don't even remember that they were at the club meetings. As for the others that you're referring to, well, very often the government had to perhaps explain a particular government, a government representative would do that. Very often somebody from the Presidency would have to say what something was about. The club was certainly very autonomous, both in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Republika Srpska, because deputies thought that their role was very important and they didn't allow anyone to dictate anything to them, Karadzic or Plavsic or anybody else. They were even more relaxed at club meetings. So it was far more difficult to streamline views than at formal sessions. But there were guests who helped the club, that's right, and even a record was kept. I think even minutes were kept in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Yes. But I think in the Serb Assembly, too, there were minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the proportion of SDS MPs in Republika Srpska who were also member of the Deputies' Club? Were all MPs attending or were only part of them, you know, the one that are more involved that were part of it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. All MPs were in the Deputies' Club. Every member of parliament was a member of the club. It wasn't that there was anybody apart, I mean in Bosnia-Herzegovina and here in the Serb Assembly. There wasn't anybody who was outside the club.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you, Mr. Krajisnik, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's quarter to 4.00. We'll have a break of half an hour to quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it the parties received the report we earlier spoke about. Then Judge Canivell will continue with questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, I would like to ask you a few questions. I know the history of your country. I would like to know what was the -- questions about yourself. I don't really want to know exactly what happened to you, you know, yourself, but I would like to know in a broader sense what exactly happened to you. I would like to know more things about your country, because you know your country went through complicated times in terms of politics and that the Balkan peninsula had been occupied by the Ottoman Empire at one time. Around the end of the 19th century Bosnia-Herzegovina turned from being under the Ottoman Empire to being under the Austro-Hungarian Empire. But after World War I, that's what I'm really interested in. What was the situation of the Muslims in your country after World War I? I mean, after World War I, Muslims were a group in a country -- you know, that they used to be members of the country that occupied Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Ottoman Empire, ages ago, and then after World War I the occupying power was an ally to the Central Empires. So after World War I these Muslims who used to be -- who used to belong to the occupying power, the Turks before, and now they were -- they had been defeated in 1918, and I guess that they had to live through difficult times because they became a minority in a state -- in this Yugoslav state -- I mean, even -- they were not even recognised in the name of the country being Muslims and this being the Yugoslav state, the state of the southern Slavs. So these Muslims -- I mean, how exactly did they feel in this new country that had been created after 1918?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the former Yugoslavia one, second, or the third one that began in 1918 is full of history. And to your question, Your Honour, I would say this: When the southern Slavs united, they were considered as Slavs who adopted Islam. There were some people who were left behind after the withdrawal of the Ottoman Empire but they were considered as Slavs and I don't know what rights they enjoyed then because at that time the prevailing distinction was between Catholics, Orthodox, and Muslims, rather than Croats, Serbs, and Muslims. The Kingdom of Yugoslavia was organised in the so-called Banovinas. I'll give you an example. In Zabrdje, where I was born, the vice-ban, like the vice-president, was a Muslim, Hadzi Omerovic. He had his country house. Back then, and later, the Muslims had an identity problem. It would take being in their shoes to give you a really objective answer as to how they felt, but it must not be easy to be in a position where two leading nations, the Serbs and the Croats, are there with you in the middle. Whether they had adopted Islam by force or of their own will, whether they were Slavs or not, it was a problem. This balance and this reciprocity was the same in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, just as before this war. People tried to show tolerance and understanding before the war, but it took very little when the war began for a rift to occur. I don't know how objective I can be, but I can understand that it's difficult when you can't find your own identity. After the Second World War, by the way, Muslims were again not recognised as a nation. They were like undecided, so they were either Serbs or Croats. And they had this persistent ambition to realise their own identity, until in the 1950s, 1950-something, I don't know which year, the former president, Tito, recognised Muslims as a nation. In this latest war that is relevant to this trial, they said: We are not Muslims, we are Bosniaks. So this constant quest for identity reoccurred as a problem. At one point they told themselves: This is our chance to get Bosnia as our state, like Serbs have their own state and Croats have their own state, because they had never had their state before. And because this ambition went unrealised for so long, this desire was stronger than anything conscious. Every unfulfilled ambition can lead to such excess. Imagine a small nation of only 2 million, they thought it was a great thing to be, although it should have been great for the Turks. When they are called "Turks," they understand that to be a derogatory term, the equivalent of the term "Chetnik" for Serbs, although it shouldn't be derogatory; on the contrary, because Turks are a great nation and a big nation. So whenever there is an upheaval, those historical antagonism and animosities come to the surface and lead to war. Bosnia used to be called miniature Yugoslavia. And at a time when Yugoslavia was being torn apart, it was difficult for Bosnia to stay together. It's difficult to me to speak in their name. I can say that I understand them, although I believe they were wrong in going against the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that is one of the main reasons for this war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You're telling me that in a derogatory way these be called Turks, so this confirms the possibility that in all that time between the two world wars and after the Second World War, socially, despite, you know, the fact that what you told us -- you know, for example, in your family people would welcome Muslims and have dinner with them, and so normally it wasn't the case. It seems in the normal state of things it was always different, always these people who felt that they weren't Muslim Turks but they had become Muslims, maybe because it was easier for them to be under the Turkish domination at one point in time. But all this determined the way they -- the -- determined the fact that they felt that the others had contempt towards this ethnic group, towards the Muslims. They felt, you know, that the others only had contempt for them because for centuries it had a different religion, and especially after the small Serbia, after World War I, transformed itself into a major Yugoslavia. So socially, how were Muslims seen by the others? Was it normal -- for example, when a Serb or a Croat would marry a Muslim -- of course you told us about a few cases yesterday, you know, where things went well, but was that seen as normal? Obviously you told us, you know, that you had good Muslims friends, but wasn't it the opposite that was more of a general rule?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. As far as marriage is concerned, there were marriages between Serbs and Muslims, Croats and Muslims, but they were in a minority, a definite minority. Marriages were usually within one ethnic group, although there were mixed marriages, of course. However, they were a definite minority, as I said. As for your suggestion that they were held in contempt, in Bosnia-Herzegovina where I lived, Muslims were predominant and played a predominant role from the liberation until this latest war. The Muslims from Bosnia have absolutely nothing to do with the Muslims that we see on television in the east. They were a peaceful people, fair, decent, and if you had any business to do, they were much easier and more pleasant to deal with than anyone else. Now, after this war, it's incredible the radicalism that appeared among the Muslims, and it's interpreted as if somebody robbed them of a state, somebody cheated them. And on account of that, people who used to be incredibly tolerant are now sowing hatred. As for what you said, it was not official and it was not public, but that point when people adopted Islam was held in disapproval by Croats and Serbs and it was held against them. But in normal, everyday life, since the 1970s when the Muslims became a majority - maybe they became a majority even earlier, I don't know - they had one area which they basically held as their dominion, that is craft and trades. Of course, a certain number of Muslims went on to university, but mainly they were in crafts and trades. Nowadays all that has changed. There are many artists and highly schooled people among the Muslims, and it is this latest war that turned Muslims into a nation. And nowadays they really feel like a nation. They have matured. If this war has brought anything good to them, it is that they feel finally as a nation. They can tell themselves: We are no longer former Serbs or former Croats, we are finally a nation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for saying this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Judge please adjust his microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to -- I'm sorry. I wasn't close enough to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are both at a disadvantage. I can't see you either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So on the one hand there was resistance to this -- the resistance of this Muslim community was only in Bosnia, right? But not in the rest of former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were Muslims living in Serbia, in an area that Serbs called Raska and Muslims call the same area Sandzak. It is closer to Kosovo. But Bosniaks are now called in Muslims in Serbia, in Croatia, and in Bosnia, although earlier, while they were still Muslims, they were only in Bosnia. Nowadays they identify themselves as Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for reminding me. Another question now that I find it hard to understand. At the end of World War II it seems that there was some kind of a genocide carried out against the Serbs, and I think I understood that this was done by Ustashi. So were they Muslim Ustashas? I am a bit confused here because I thought there were only Ustashas. Muslims were aside and -- were they involved in this or not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were Muslims among the Ustashas. Croats called them Croats of Muslim faith, and there was even a notorious Muslim division called the Handzar Division. They wore their caps that are part of their national costume, but they were Ustashas on the Croat side. There were, however, some Muslims among the partisans but also among the Chetniks, although very few because the Chetniks were derived from the old Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the situation that existed at the end of World War II, can't you say that it cropped up again at -- during the war, you know, that we're interested in, because there was more of a divide between the -- with the Croat -- with the Muslims. Or is it because the Muslims were more numerous in Bosnia than the Croats? How should I try and understand this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croats and Muslims, from the very beginning of multi-party political life formed a coalition. Although they were sharing power with the SDS, they immediately sided together and left the SDS on the other side. And when the war began, they were already together. At a certain point, I don't know whether it was at the end of 1992 or in 1993, they started infighting over some territories or over some crimes, and a war began between Muslims and Croats. At the end of the war, however, the Federation was formed, comprised of Muslims and Croats, but it is not a marriage based on love. There is antagonism against -- among Croats and Muslims, just among Croats and Serbs, and Serbs and Muslims. The Croats now believe that they are disenfranchised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was the independence of Croatia, and chronologically that happened before the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you think that that was a reason -- that was a -- sort of triggered what happened in Bosnia later on? Because apparently they were supposed to respect the borders, you know, that were already there after the -- between the six republics that had been set up after World War II. So did you think that this complicated -- this was a reason -- this was one of the reasons for the complications that occurred later on, the fact that they wanted to make a state with the -- using the territories that used to be Bosnia-Herzegovina before and the -- because they couldn't -- the Serbs wanted to be with the -- maybe with the other Serbs that were in other former Yugoslavian states, but because of the borders the way they were they couldn't do it anymore.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I always take it into account that I may not be entirely objective, but it's up to you to judge that. I believe that Muslims were instigated by Croats to go forward with the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as it were, and I believe that the war was imported from Croatia into Bosnia and Herzegovina. Croatia found it a relief because it had a war with the Serbs in Krajina, and they wanted to take some territories in the west and in the north, like Posavina. During negotiations I talked to Croat representatives. It was their opinion that it was important for them in those areas where they had authority and control, whereas the other things would be left for some later stage. I'm absolutely certain that if the Serbs and Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina could have their way, they would both join Serbia and Croatia respectively, whereas the Muslims would either have liked to have all of Bosnia or would liked to have the most prosperous part of Bosnia for their state. This is my perspective from here in The Hague and of course the wisdom of hindsight when I look back on some conversations that I had with them. Both Serbs and Croats are all the nations who had lived there for centuries, and they remember what happened 300, 500 years back. And in the Second World War, the Serbs suffered a lot, including from genocide, and especially in the regions that we have referred to a lot during this trial. The Ustashas massacred people in Mount Kozara area, the Jasenovac concentration camp, et cetera. Of course Muslims also remember being victimised in Eastern Bosnia by the Chetniks. So everybody has their own history and everybody looks back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's for a general aspect. Now, if we go into more details, you said in your testimony that there was a referendum in November 1991. I think I've understood -- I'm not sure I understood. This was done along with the constitution; is that what happened? Or is it the Serbs who decided to call for a referendum in order to know who was in favour, who was against the situation as it was at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not in accordance with the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In actual fact, when there was this rift in the Assembly on the 14th of October, the SDS was advocating the following view: That the Muslims and the Croats did not have the right to declare the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina on their own and that the SDS is the legitimate representative of the Serb people. And they said what it was that the Serbs wanted. They wanted Bosnia-Herzegovina to remain within Yugoslavia. Then objections were voiced in terms of the SDS not having legitimacy because there were Serbs in other political parties, too. It was then that the Assembly of the Serb People was established, and they called a plebiscite in order to see what the will of the Serb people was. Others voted, too, and then it was said: Well, now you have information about what the Serb people think. It wasn't compulsory, this plebiscite, but it was there to show whether that policy pursued by the SDS had a certain legitimacy. Actually, there is this one particular provision, the so-called self-determination of peoples. It is a provision, but it was not really elaborated upon in the constitution that you had the right to resort to, say, a plebiscite and to carry this through in that way, because this was actually never done in socialism, and this constitution dated back to the days of socialism. Well, perhaps it was legitimate, but it was not legal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand the difference. But it was a referendum called by the SDS, and the only ones who could take part in it were the ethnic Serbs. The others weren't even allowed to take part in the vote, the Muslims and the Croats were not allowed to take part in the vote. Okay. Then there's another question which might be interesting --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, everybody could take part in it, but there were a certain type of ballots for Serbs who were in favour of Yugoslavia; a second type for Croats; a third type for Muslims, so that others could state their views, too, in terms of Bosnia remaining in Yugoslavia. However, the absolute majority of voters who took part in it were Serbs. And Yugoslavs as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Muslims and Croats didn't vote in that referendum, or did they vote? I don't think any Muslims or Croats participated in the vote?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few non-Serbs voted in the referendum or people who did not declare themselves as Yugoslavs. It was just a very small percentage of Croats and Muslims who voted in the referendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you told us in your testimony that when -- on the May 12th -- in the Assembly that you chaired on May 12th, 1992, you voted on the six strategic goals and on your future and what -- as you said, that was important in order to have something to negotiate on, to negotiate on with the other -- with the international community and with the other ethnicities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But I'd like to ask you the following question: But wasn't that going to stimulate what was going to happen? Wasn't it going to trigger what was going to happen? A war. The fact, you know, that these six strategic goals could be achieved in another way then through negotiation -- actually, through war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had been in a war for a month already. These goals were presented when we presented our requests to Mr. Cutileiro, namely that we wanted to have a constituent unit of our own, that we wanted it to be linked up, and so on and so forth. That is to say that these were objections voiced by the MPs, they were saying that they often did not know what it was that we advocated in the negotiations. Then what was stated was what we actually wanted. There is even a book called: "What do the Serbs want?" And it was published. This is actually a platform on the basis of which we had already worked with Cutileiro. So these six strategic goals were adopted, but at the same session we adopted the conclusions, stating that we wanted the conference to continue and that we wanted it to go on until a political solution is reached. You can read that from the session of the 12th of May, because we knew if we do not verify something in a political way it doesn't matter how you actually fair in war -- I mean, war brings you nothing, it brings you only victims. That was our objective on the 12th of May, and we did not vote about the strategic objectives; we voted about the entire information presented, not about the goals specifically. Within this information, they were incorporated, too. It's a different matter altogether that later on they were published as a document; I explained that in 1993 -- well, I don't know. Perhaps they were adopted on purpose or by mistake. It wasn't on my part at any rate, but they were published, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am -- then you continue to try and find solutions, negotiated solutions, you know, to find -- even though, as you say, the war had already broken out a month before that statement where you announced the six strategic objectives. But afterwards -- well, you especially were negotiating, you knew that at the same time these objectives had influence -- had an influence on the war that was going on, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it can be taken that way, but believe me, ewe never knew what you could achieve while the war was still on. The fortunes of war changed to such an extent and ultimately -- well, I don't know. Apart from one particular objective, I don't think that any one of these objectives were attained. You simply have no idea what tomorrow will bring because the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina is the front. So every municipality had a plan of its own. If they could take a village of their own or whatever else, quite simply, there was this confederacy, if I can put it that way, a confederacy of goals. Everybody had a goal of their own, a local goal of their own. This was a platform for negotiations, and now what could you achieve if there is a war on? That depended on the fortunes of war. You would gain a few, lose a few. War is, well, something that is either imposed or not imposed; you either want it or you don't want it. I mean, nobody wants a war, but once a war starts it is hard to stop it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Then you also told us that you were in favour -- you were in favour of -- you thought that the changes in population had to be done deliberately. I mean, you wanted only those to leave -- those who left their territories to be people who wanted to leave their territories. That's what you said many times. So you only wanted, you know, movements of population to be done through the will of the people, but at the same time you seem to think that that was an acceptable way of doing things, but you knew that there was a war going on also. So didn't the fact that there was a war going on sort of force people to leave on both sides? So people -- you say that people were leaving of their free will, but it wasn't that free. They were leaving because there was a war. Maybe for other reasons, but they were leaving because of the war. Isn't that obvious for you that that's why people were leaving?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when there is a war going on, the most important thing is to stay alive. The easiest thing in a war is to lose one's life; it's easier than anything else. When I talked about Serbs who were leaving Central Bosnia, when they were leaving their homes and when they were happy, I understood them. During the course of the negotiations, during those four years, 20 times or perhaps even more than that I thought: We've achieved peace. Practically at every conference you would think: Yes, this has brought the war to an end. You're absolutely right. People flee from war, especially those who are a minority. They want to save their lives, and they hope that the war would end quickly. That's what happened in the Second World War, people fled from certain areas, the war was over, and then everybody went back home where they had lived. This turned out to be quite different. I was happy when, say, these Serbs -- when I saw that they got out alive. Believe me, those who stayed on in territories where they were a minority fared much worse than those who had left; I'm talking about Sarajevo, Zenica, Tuzla, I don't know, other areas as well. When you are a minority for a long time, there are various elements that get out of control and therefore your life is in jeopardy and it is hard to stay alive. I have the example of a Croat doctor in Pale who came to ask me for help. And I said: Yes, tell me. And he said: Well, I have this friend. And that is when I called this Malko Koroman, I remember, and he said: I'll find these criminals. This was a doctor, a paediatrician, who had treated many, many Serb children, and a criminal threatened him. Thank goodness he stayed alive. He survived and he wanted to be a witness here, in fact, but he died a month or two ago. What I'm trying to say is that in every environment there are people who could jeopardise your life. If people were moving out under force, that was all -- that was not right. If people left of their own accord, then it's different. I'm a refugee myself, and I know what it's like to leave your home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also said during your testimony that you did not know of serious offences made to human rights and serious breaches of human rights that occurred, despite, I imagine- that what I'm asking - that you often left your country, you attended international meetings. So during these international meetings wasn't -- didn't you -- weren't you able to say: What's going on? What's happening out -- you know, what's happening in terms of human rights? During these negotiations, first with Lord Carrington and Cutileiro and then later on with Vance Owen, didn't the people who were there never -- didn't it ever occur to them to ask: What's going on? Do you know what's going on? Can you -- what can you do to stop what's happening in the country? Didn't that ever occur?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that here. There were complaints made by the representatives of the international community that there was ethnic cleansing, that there were persecutions, and other things, too, camps, and so on. I told you, there were people who were in charge of things, like the MUP and people from the Presidency, and they were in contact with certain structures. I would always receive information. We discussed that at this consultative meeting. Information -- the information that we got was that this was propaganda, that things were actually the other way around. And when a commission was established, when they went to the area and communications were very poor, then some things were actually discovered. And this seemed to be only a small part of the problem, for instance that there were prisons but not that there were murders. And measures were taken, very strict measures. I don't want to commit a sin. This was not my area of responsibility, but the government, the Presidency, I felt that everybody wanted to have the rule of law established and to have perpetrators punished. Nobody supported that, but it is incredible the extent to which crimes were being concealed. I told you about Sarajevo, a diameter of 2 kilometres, and the authorities did not know what was going on there, in that area. A crime could happen in the building next door, you wouldn't know during the course of a war. Quite simply, people who committed crimes hid that and you did not have sufficient information, you could not investigate that, the judiciary was not functioning properly, and it was only later on that you would find out what had happened. So I know that whenever accusations were made, there was always a discussion and measures were always taken. I do not remember a single meeting where this was on the agenda and when measures were not taken later on, to establish the truth, to punish the persons who were guilty -- I mean, I simply do not remember a meeting where somebody said it doesn't matter, never mind what happened. And in addition to that I'll tell you something else. I had my own family problems. While my wife was alive, I had that problem; and then I had three children. They were in Pale and I spent most of my time in Pale. I didn't travel that much, except that I attended Assembly meetings. So I could not tour the entire area, so I could not establish -- I mean, that I myself could establish what the truth was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you say that there are many crimes that were hidden, maybe so. But there were other situations that were shown to the entire world on the media, especially with the -- you know, this -- on TV. So when you left the country, when you went to London, to Brussels, you told us that in July you went to London, in July of 1992. I think there was another meeting at the end of August, also in London, and another one in Geneva later on. Didn't that strike you, just in passing in front of a TV, to see that on the screen, people coming to ask -- asking: What's happening? What's going on? Didn't it occur to you that you could ask what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I was highly interested in what was going on. At these meetings that we attended, everything that was presented -- say this meeting in London, conclusions were reached, decisions were reached to disband all prisons and to have all persons exchanged. Then somebody was supposed to carry this through and some things were indeed carried out. I know that, for example, if there were such accusations made, then those who were in charge, say Karadzic, Koljevic, would present certain views on that, and indeed they had the same kind of information that I did. I cannot say anything that wouldn't be right, and they probably got this information from people they had consulted previously. Regrettably, in the media, in foreign media, there were some things that we knew were not true. For example, they would show a graveyard full of crosses and then they would say - I heard that - this is the graveyard of Muslims that were killed by the Serbs. We know that Muslims do not have crosses on their tombstones. So for somebody out there, that may seem to be true. But then you feel that there is no objectivity in information. So I heard about that, and then you get the impression that everything is rigged and that everything is false. You saw Mrs. Plavsic's open letter. She said: It is not correct. There are Muslims that -- there are also Muslim organised camps and so on and so forth, and it is not civilians who are in prisons and so on and so forth. I mean, I'm just saying that the situation was the same on other sides, too. Quite simply, there was chaos all over the place and where authority was brought down to the lowest possible level and very often was in the hands of highly responsible people. We started from scratch, basically, when we started building some kind of a legal system. I'm not trying to justify people who were in charge of this, but that's just the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but for example there was a moment where Mr. Karadzic -- I don't remember if he learned it through the Times or some minister of -- explaining that there were Arab attacks and he said: Well, this is all fabrication. But did he have intelligence or something? Because when you say, okay, somebody's been killed. You say: No, it's not true. And you can deny it. But the opposite is difficult, saying that this has not occurred. So how did he make that statement so quickly? Did he investigate, you know? I mean, you were always with him, so did you know what happened when he made that statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that statement -- well, maybe my conclusions are wrong. I'm not Mr. Karadzic's lawyer; I'm defending myself. As far as I knew, information could come from the MUP, from the military, and perhaps for -- from people who were in the field. But I hadn't heard of anybody confirming such reports. If Karadzic received the same information, then perhaps he reacted on the basis of that, and then later on you established that there was something wrong and that some chief of police had misinformed you or something. Well, he informed his minister and the minister misinformed you. I mean, I'm talking about the persons who were actually in charge of such things. There is one thing, Your Honour, I myself, I personally, could not punish anyone, could not promote anyone, I could not give anyone a decoration, I could not give anyone a commendation. Had I received some information - I've already given you an example - I would certainly want for my own sake, as a human being, to see this through. Not because it was my duty. I wouldn't want anything to remain unresolved because that would give my people and the policy that I take part in a bad name. But had I known of any such thing, I would have reacted and I always reacted in order to have things investigated to the very end if there were indications. However, I do not want to commit a sin. I should say that others reacted, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and finally, you said in your testimony that when you were meeting in the Presidency of Republika Srpska you were always there as a guest, you always attended those meetings as a guest. So I think you were there in almost all the meetings except for one, all the meetings of this Presidency from January all the way to December. So I would like to know what it meant to be a guest at those meetings. What did you do exactly? What was the role that you played in those meetings as a guest?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not think that these were meetings of the Presidency. I first saw these records here, in The Hague. I knew that there were certain reminders. I thought that these were consultative meetings. Very often we had consultative meetings. We'd discuss various problems, various respective problems. As for these consultative meetings, I'm the "guilty party," and Mr. Djeric, too, because we simply wanted to consult about certain matters. Because I used to work in a company where we would have senior staff meetings, we'd discuss a problem, and then everybody would go and do his own job. We would discuss various problems there. There were many decisions that were reached, say of the Presidency, that were not reached at these meetings; they were reached autonomously. For example, all orders issued by Mr. Karadzic were issued apart from these meetings. Then there were laws and other things that were not part of the agenda of these meetings. After all, that is his right -- or rather, the right of the Presidency. Now, whether they had any separate meetings -- well, I think that was very seldom. These were sort of ad hoc meetings. They were not particularly official meetings. At these meetings that were called Presidency meetings, there was this discussion, debate, about all sorts of things. And, quite simply, if somebody had a particular task or a particular problem, we'd discuss it and then everybody'd go and do his own work. I did not take over anything from the Presidency. I never did anything that was not part of my own job. I would not allow myself to be part of an illegal body. If they want me to become a member of a particular body, have the Assembly vote on it.
