And if the Assembly votes and says that I'm a member of the Presidency, then all right. But, I mean, I would not do it any other way. We were all there, we consulted on problems and our jobs. I remember most of the items that were on the agenda, and then after that we all went out and did our own work. I didn't know what the government did. They didn't know what I did. Others didn't know either, then everybody went off and did their own work. Very often these meetings were brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but how can you explain that in the minutes of what happened over there the mention is decisions made on problems, you know, appointment of this person, appointment of commissioners to Crisis Staffs or to war staffs? And at one point in time also if I remember on June 27th, 1992, at the meeting of the Presidency and in the minutes that we got, it was -- General Mladic was ordered to stop bombing Sarajevo, not just that, it wasn't a consultation, you know, it was a decision, it was an order, that was given to General Mladic. And after that order given to General Mladic, bombing actually stopped, right there. So how -- it looks like these meetings were decision-making meetings. They weren't just consultative meetings, at least from what we saw, it definitely looks like they were decision-making meetings.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that refers to a meeting that was not attended by Karadzic but was attended by Koljevic, Plavsic, Djeric, and I, and when we said that firing at Dobrinja should stop -- I mean Sarajevo, and that the Supreme Command should be told to issue orders to the Main Staff to that effect. It's probably the case that somebody who was in contact with the UNPROFOR received complaints about Sarajevo being shelled -- or maybe somebody said the conference can't go on because the Serbs are attacking the city, and Koljevic presented that at the meeting. And it was concluded that regardless of the crime that it constituted, it did us political damage and that indeed the Presidency should issue orders to stop that, regardless of whether the military had any excuse for that or not. The recording secretary wrote that, not because the order was issued then and there, the orders were issued in due course by whoever was in charge. But the Presidency did note that such an order should be issued because it was doing us political damage. The military justification was maybe there, but it was doing us political damage because the conference could not go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you mean that in these meetings decisions were never made, except by those who were in the Presidency, Koljevic and you didn't mention Mrs. Plavsic. But there was a meeting in November 1992 where the three members of the Presidency were present. So how were the decisions made then when there were only one person who was able to make the decision --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that meeting the only person available to make the decision was one of the members of the Presidency; the two others were only consultative.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that speaks volumes. A certain problem would be discussed, and if the problem fell into the jurisdiction of the Presidency, the Presidency would decide. If it fell within the province of the Assembly, the Assembly would deal with it. The same goes for the government. And the implementation would be up to the competent body, whether it would be by an order, whether it would be placed on the agenda. The initiative would come from the competent body. It would be placed on the agenda to hear the opinion of others, but the implementation was always in the hands of the body in charge. I, for instance, could not issue orders to the army to stop the shelling. It could be done by the president of the Presidency, as the supreme commander, just like they could not preside over an Assembly session. The same is true of the government. I, for instance, did not attend a single cabinet meeting. I don't know what was decided there because finally it was -- I mean, in 1992 it was their province. But it was quite normal for them to attend Assembly sessions when I presided and members of the Presidency attended, too, although because they not have the right of vote at Assembly sessions. Only MPs had the right to vote. But we were anxious to hear their opinion when they rose to spoke to tell us their opinion. Of course, the MPs appreciated that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'll not start right away with my questions because we'll first have a break. But I have one follow-up question for you. One of your last answers to Judge Canivell's question you responded in the following way. You said: If that refers to a meeting that was not attended by Mr. Karadzic, but -- and then you mentioned those who were present. "And when we said that firing at Dobrinja should stop, I mean Sarajevo, and that the Supreme Command should be told to issue orders to the Main Staff to that effect, it is probably the case that somebody," and then you continued. I think correctly you said "and when we said," because if we read what it says, it says: "The Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic of BH is ordered to cease all infantry and military operations in the suburb of Dobrinja immediately." Do we immediately that at least the text, the language, does not say that you are asking the Supreme Command to issue orders to the Main Staff, but that, at least in this text, there was a direct order to the Main Staff to act immediately. That's what it says, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Maybe on page 2, I think. You have it in some record that the Main Staff should report to the Supreme Command or seek information. If I had that record I could answer this. It's difficult to say something like this off the cuff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If someone would have the B/C/S version of the 12th Presidency Session of the 27th of June, then we could -- it's P65, tab 171, I take it. Yes. Yes, could it be given to Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik, I have in front of me the minutes of the 12th Session, and I was referring to paragraph 3, first full sentence, which reads in English, but if it's not well translated then we have to verify that: "The Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic of BH is ordered to cease all artillery and infantry operations in the suburb of Dobrinja immediately."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It says: "The Main Staff is ordered." But it's not an order. This is up to somebody to implement after this because there was no representative of the Main Staff. Somebody had to write out an order, somebody in the Presidency, and to send them that order. And it must be linked with this last item where the Main Staff is instructed to establish contact with the UNPROFOR and start implementing -- no, sorry, the previous one. "Fire is to be opened only in necessary defence" -- that's what I meant. "Fire is to be opened only for necessary defence, but only with prior notification to the Supreme Command and the UNPROFOR is the mediator in the airport operation." This is what I mean. This is just a memo because Karadzic was not there. It's probably the case that somebody said: The Main Staff should be ordered immediately to stop this, and the recording secretary wrote it down. But this is not the way you write orders. Somebody should -- somebody over there should have written it and sent it to the Main Staff. If the representative of the Main Staff was there, then you could say that he heard this, but normally an order is not written this way. It had to be an order in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, it also could be read, I'm just putting this to you, that an order was given to cease all artillery and infantry operations immediately, that -- as the second line says, that the armed forces should move from offensive to defensive positions, which at least suggests that they were in offensive positions. And that, for the future, fire should be opened only for necessary defence, after having consulted with the Presidency, the Supreme Command, and UNPROFOR. So apart from whether the Presidency and the Supreme Command both played a role there. But you could also read it as making a clear distinction between orders that took immediate effect and orders that would need further consultation, that is to respond to open fire only for necessary defence.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this is not an order. On the basis of this paper, somebody was to write out an order, the competent body was to write an order and approve this. It's true that two members of the Presidency were present, but this was to serve only as a basis for further enactments. That's why it was a consultative meeting. Yes, we could have noted whatever we saw fit, but somebody else was to write an order. This is not enough. This is not something received by the -- or receivable by the Main Staff or the Supreme Command. The Main Staff did not receive this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, that's not what the text says. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we agree, we agree completely. It's written just as you said, but after this somebody was to write an order to implement this. The Main Staff did not receive this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second portion of your reasoning is that you say: "This was to serve only as a basis for further enactments." Then you said: "That's why it was a consultative meeting." Here your assumption or your testimony that it was a consultative meeting explains why something was still to be done. That also means that if it was not a consultative meeting, that that reasoning is not valid anymore.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You see, this is a consultative meeting, not an advisory meeting. People consult each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where does it say so? Could you please tell me, this is decision A, decision B, order A, order B. Where does it say -- I mean, you have repeatedly told us that, and one of the things which is very important is that you gave your interpretation of the text on the basis of what you say what is your knowledge, but of course the Judges have their own responsibility in interpreting texts and to see whether the text support your testimony in this respect. So therefore I'm inviting you to give us those portions of the text that clearly indicate that these were consultative meetings rather than decision -- rather than meetings where decisions were taken, because the text so often says: Decision this, order that. So if you would assist us in -- help us in finding textual support for your interpretation of these texts and your recollection of what happened during those meetings, then it would highly -- be highly appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, Mr. President, you see this paper was signed by Mr. Karadzic; it means that it was typed out later. Because we, when we hold the meeting, somebody takes notes, and afterwards writes it all out. Especially when Karadzic was not present, he wrote it out the next day or even later. When I say that it was a consultative meeting, it's not written anywhere that it was a consultative meeting. It says: "A meeting of the Presidency in immediate threat of war," not in a state of war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the attendees discussed things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're now mixing up a few things. I think I never put it to you that it said that it was during a state of war. I'm just asking you to point at those portions in the text which would support your testimony that these were consultative meetings, and I just heard you say that the text doesn't say so.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not written in the text, but look where it says: To hold a patron saint's day, for one of them to go to Ilijas, for a delegation of the government to go -- it's not even specified who should be on the delegation. There were lots of such conclusions. This thing should be done and that thing should be done, et cetera. Things should be done is the wording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you say it's not even said who would be in the delegation. I see under 1 that for St. Vitus day, the patron saint for the army of the Serbian Republic, the following appointees go, under A: For Han Pijesak, Biljana Plavsic, Dr. Branko Djeric, and Bogdan Subotic. B: For Ilijas Dr. Nikola Koljevic and Momcilo Krajisnik. C: For Res [phoen] Velobar Ostojic and Ljubomir Zukovic. Your testimony just was that it wasn't even said who would be the delegates. Could you explain to me -- and you took this example, how could I read it in such a way that the delegates were not even, as you said -- let me just check that. "It's not even specified who should be on the delegation." I see for all three delegations, I see persons clearly mentioned to be on that delegations.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I meant is this: The government is instructed to appoint a delegation to tour military units and hospitals. Here, the government is urged to appoint units to visit military units and hospital. We were there and we were talking about who should go to some sort of celebration. It was not a decision; it was simply an understanding between us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that the decision is laid in the hands of the government. We'll first have a break. We'll resume at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I've got a few questions for you as well. First of all, you explained many, many times that it was unconstitutional what the -- the Muslims and the Croats did in the way they sought independence for BiH. Could you tell us what would have been the constitutional way to do it, step by step. What would have been needed in accordance with the constitution to gain independence?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Independence could have taken place only by way of changing the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And how would you change the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the constitution would be changed in the following way. The constitutional commission would, well, provide a draft and then there would be a public debate and then a proposal would be presented, and this would go to the Assembly. And two-thirds from both chambers, that is to say the Chamber of Nations and the Chamber of Citizens, two -- there would have to be a two-third majority that would vote in favour of the new constitution that would provide for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is what Slovenia and Croatia had done; before that, they had had a referendum to see what the public thought and felt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So do I understand well that so a minority could have blocked independence if it was at least one-third of the vote? Is that correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A change of the constitution, yes. But there was an instrument perhaps; that's very important. In fact, national questions, questions that were of vital interest, could not be, well, voted on until this would be considered by the council for the national and ethnic equality of peoples, and it would be that council that would have to pass a two-thirds decision. And once there is such a decision, then the proposal will be presented to the Assembly, and then two-thirds of the MPs will have to support that decision made by the council. Something similar is in place in Bosnia-Herzegovina now with regard to these questions -- well, there's actually a council of peoples rather than this original council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this council for national equality, there in that council, a minority could have blocked a way to independence. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in terms of vital national interests, that is to say a minority could do that -- well, they could not discuss any issue, laws, or whatever. But as for vital interests, a minority could block a majority. This exists to this day -- or rather, it was introduced after Dayton. What was insisted upon was consensus and accommodation of views rather than out-voting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you consider that a question of independence could be resolved by a consensus, where the parties were so much opposing each other?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that we absolutely could have done it that way, and I can even explain how.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had two extremes. Say the Serbs wanted Yugoslavia and the Muslims wanted an independent, unitary state. The Croats were sort of in between. Agreement was reached, either under pressure or by way of a reality. You recognise Bosnia and you give up on Yugoslavia and agree that Bosnia will be a complex national community like Switzerland, Belgium, and so on. So those are the principles involved, and on the basis of that there could have been an independent Bosnia without any war. People were delighted when these principles were agreed upon. People did not want war. And I think that this is a great pity, historically speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, things went otherwise. A constitutional solution was not found. Now, looking at the new situation in the Republika Srpska - and I'm first concentrating on the central level - how were the minorities represented on the central level, be it government, be it Assembly, be it Presidency, in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean once the war started?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Once the Republika Srpska was established and that the war started soon after that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Republika Srpska was established on the 9th of January, 1992. That is to say two or three months before the war. It was established on paper - on paper - that is to say it was almost a fiction. On the 25th of January, so that is to say just a bit after that, there was an Assembly meeting of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the referendum, and I asked the MPs through my own authority to go to this joint Assembly. And we discussed this for two days, to see how the Serbs could take part in the referendum, too, and indeed we found a solution. The government agreed on regionalisation. There is a recording of that and there is a transcript, too. That would have satisfied the Serbs. So we all would have taken part in the referendum, Bosnia would have been independent, but we would have had these units, these constituent units. Of course that is what was supposed to be done. And you even have this decision, that is to say the deputy Prime Minister, Mr. Cengic, who was also vice-president of the SDA. He went to the rostrum together with Karadzic and he said: We've reached agreement. And everybody was so pleased. However, after that, Mr. Izetbegovic went back on that and said: We give up on this. That was the last session of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was held. So agreement was reached at 3.00 at night. I had this session going on for two days, and we kept discussing and trying to reach agreement, and that was the last chance to avoid everything. And then there was Cutileiro and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But My question was how the minorities were represented.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that on the 9th of January Republika Srpska existed only on paper. It did not actually start functioning at all until the war started. So the Muslims and Croats did not even take part in this state that existed only on paper. No territory, no nothing, you just have this proclamation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now things moved on. At a certain moment there was a territory, there was -- there was an Assembly. What steps were taken then to have the Muslims and the Croats represented in the newly established organs of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have an example, say of an attempt. Mr. Kupresanin asked an MP, a Muslim, to enter the Assembly. He came to Banja Luka, and he had had contact with Karadzic over the telephone. You have a recording here, and he said: Please, join the Assembly because you're from Banja Luka and you're from that old Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Apparently he agreed to that, but later on he refused. MPs from the HDZ and the SDA did not want to take part in this "artificial" Assembly. During the war, whether we like it or not, it was exclusively Serb. I'm talking about the authorities at the level of Republika Srpska. That's what you asked me about. But say at municipal level, Mr. President -- well, and this is a smaller part. For example, in Banja Luka the vice-president was a Croat and then there was some Muslims, but only at first. Later on, quite simply, there weren't any, like on the other side, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now in some municipalities where the Muslims were a majority, for example in Prijedor, what -- what happened there as far as the rights of Muslims and Croats were concerned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you saw Mr. Srdic's statement here, that they did all of that on their own, that we did not have any contact with Prijedor until the end of June because there was no communication. So what was done? They got into a fight. Without a war, the Serb side took the municipality, and then the fight broke out, that is to say the war broke out. I don't think that the Assembly operated at all. They had a Crisis Staff or a Presidency. I learned that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you've told us that Serb Assemblies had to be formed in the municipalities. They were mainly, as you told us -- were an instrument to express the views of Serbs on vital issues, vital to them, not for any decision-making. Could you tell us: What happened later with these Serb Assemblies? Did they ever in a later stage -- not necessarily before the year 1992. Did they function? Did they finally play a role as an Assembly or ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean during the war? I did not quite understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you said it was -- these Assemblies, these Serb Assemblies, were formed. Of course we know about Crisis Staffs, we know about war commissions or War Presidencies, but what exactly happened with these Serb Assemblies? Did they ever function as an Assembly at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a later stage in most municipalities, yes. Practically in all by the end of 1992, the organs of government, if I can put it that way, started to function, the executive councils, the Executive Boards of municipalities that consisted of Serbs, of course for the most part, during the war. So there weren't any commissions or commissioners, so they did start functioning, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did at these later stages -- was an opportunity given to be represented in those representative bodies as an Assembly to Muslims and Croats who had remained on the territory of those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot -- well, it would be dishonest of me to try to give a quality answer now. I can give you my opinion, though. I know that we would have been glad had the Muslims from those areas been in the municipalities, and then we would have said: Well, we have mixed municipalities and Assemblies, just like the Muslims did in Sarajevo with just a couple of Serbs. But that simply didn't happen. Even those who were in the Assembly left. So there was an absolute majority of Serbs, although I know the policy was it would be a welcome thing if we were only to look at politics -- of course we'd be happy if we had members of the Municipal Assembly who were not Serbs. But the same goes for the other side. But never mind about the other side; I'm talking about the Serb side now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Wasn't this a constitutionally guaranteed right to be represented on the local level?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are absolutely right. We had the most democratic of constitutions. But there was a war and, quite simply, this was a utopia. You could not carry it through. Well, after the war, yes, but not during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the right to be represented in directly elected representative bodies was a dead letter at that moment. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, there were no elections during the course of the war. There were only old Assemblymen from 1990. They were not in parliament. For the most part, they didn't want to be there. They left that parliament where Republika Srpska was, if I could put it that way. However, they certainly would have been received had they been willing to join the parliament, the municipal parliament, I mean. The republican parliament, too, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was any, apart from that telephone call you just referred to by Mr. Kupresanin, was any initiative taken to -- to make the rights of Muslims and Croats any more than a -- as you just confirmed this, of a dead letter.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, more was done to protect people along the lines of the Geneva Conventions and so on and so forth. Really, as far as political life is concerned there were Crisis Staffs or Presidencies or commissions. So in that period when the Assemblies started to operate, that was already the second half of 1992, perhaps even the fourth quarter of 1992. So - how should I put this? - one could not talk about a productive product, that you were involving Muslims in municipal government, although the door was always open. People were, quite simply, leaving. Serbs were leaving and, of course, Muslims and Croats, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say: "More was done to protect people along the lines of the Geneva Conventions and so on and so forth." Is my recollection correct that war crimes against Serbs were investigated?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, not investigated at all, although a commission had been established. They should have been investigated, just like a commission was established on the Muslim side for all, and as a matter of fact papers were being collected and war was being waged. I don't know whether the Serbs investigated anything against the Serbs -- I mean -- well, the central commission. I'm talking about the central commission, but I don't know about what was done at municipal level. I do not recall now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said a commission had been established to investigate although they didn't do it, to investigate war crimes committed against Serbs. Was a similar -- were similar initiatives taken in -- to investigate violations of the Geneva Conventions against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a standing order several times that if there were any indications that things should be looked into and that the perpetrators should be punished. I'm sure that this exists on paper, too, these orders. Now, how that was actually carried out in practice, that I don't know. That is a different matter. This was an enormous burden, and also that was not one's goal, to violate the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was exactly the enormous burden?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you have negotiations, and if somebody keeps accusing you of something all the time. I'm talking apart from crimes. I mean, that's not permissible, of course. Of course you do your best to investigate that and to get that out of the way because, to put it mildly, this is not in your political interests, it's not politically useful. How can that be useful if somebody is killing, raping, looting, whatever? It is not in the interests of normal politicians, especially if you want to resolve a problem by political means. Why would you be under pressure all the time? I don't know. Especially if this is being done by criminals who are robbing Serbs and who are committing crimes against the Serbs, too? Why would you protect criminals? You would not have a single reason to protect criminals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You were asked by Judge Canivell earlier on how seriously you took the media reports on -- blaming the Serbs for misbehaviour. And then you answered that by saying: Well, they would come with a graveyard with crosses on it saying: Well, these are all the Muslims that died. And of course Muslims have no crosses on their graveyards, so it is -- that was more or less the answer you gave. Did you also see information -- information which was not obviously and immediately recognisable as total nonsense?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned an example of a lack of confidence in the international media, so I referred to that. This is what the measures were: We took a statement. The minister of information took all the journalists who had written against us before that. He took them out on a trip to show that this was not true and he had a press conference in that same place, Prijedor. And his impressions when he got back were quite different. Now, was he deceived? How did this turn out to be so different? Well, journalists from all media went there and he said: Write about everything that you've seen. There's no censorship. What could I do? I could only believe or not believe him. If I would not believe him, then I would have to go to check things out and I would probably get the same information, although that was not my job, it was his job. Mr. Bozanic went, too, and that woman who was here, who was a witness here, she took journalists, too. That is what could be done, to see whether journalists were right in terms of what they were writing about or was the situation different. That what I can -- well, I don't know. What could I do? Would I have to turn into a traveller to follow in the trails of a delegation to see whether everything was correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, among the adjudicated facts we have information about serious malnutrition in some places of detention. Did you ever see the television broadcast at that time, whether you saw it directly on television or on any picture, of people that were visibly malnourished?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you're referring to the example from Prijedor, I ask you, please, there is this film here, I gave it to my Defence, where the journalist states that all of that was stage-managed. Could the Defence please find that cassette that I provided? So the journalist himself says: This is how they stage-managed all of it. So then you really have this dilemma as to what was correct out of all of this or not. Please, I gave the Defence this cassette where the man says how all of that was stage-managed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it did occur to me to suggest when Your Honour put the question, a need to be a bit more specific. I decided to wait to see whether Mr. Krajisnik, well, picked up in a way that meant that there wasn't any problem or uncertainty about what we're talking about, but it's apparent that there might be. So I would invite Your Honour to be a bit more specific than just refer to the telephone broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's there -- well, I would say it has become a notorious picture of -- I've forgotten the name. I think it is in evidence, the man who is behind the barbed wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can picture it myself. Yes, indeed, Your Honour. But Mr. Krajisnik responded by asking a question for confirmation of what was being talked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we're talking about the same, but let's get it confirmed. That's -- I've forgotten under what number it is in evidence, but the one who is standing behind barbed wire. That -- it seems that Mr. Krajisnik has the same. Yes. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, apart from to what extent that is staged, was the state of malnutrition staged as well in view of -- I mean, I was talking not primarily about who was behind the barbed wire and who was, but I'm mainly talking about the visible malnutrition of the person on the picture, was that staged as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that footage then. It was published later, and then I got curious and wanted to know what it was about. I don't know why the man looked like that. If he was thin, then obviously he didn't eat enough. But really, at that time I didn't know anything about it. Instead, I got a film in which it is explained that the man was not behind the wire fence, he was outside the wire fence. I don't know what's true, whether he was in prison and lost weight there or not, I don't know. But I really did watch that film that was broadcast on television several times later. But I didn't see it at the time, nor do I know why the man appeared like that. It would be a good idea to show that film that I have produced on a cassette. I don't know what's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not primarily interested in to what extent all the other parts were staged; I'm primarily interested in a state of malnutrition. But let's move to another subject, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Ten people around him look quite well fed, and he is really thin, that's true. All the other people around him, who are apparently in the same prison, look quite normal. So you have to wonder why he is only one who is so thin. You will -- you can have a look at that photo, and if you pay attention to the people standing next to him they are all- how shall I say? - normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to move to the next subject which is, to some extent, related to what we earlier discussed. That is the functioning of the judiciary. To what extent were you involved in the setting up or establishing the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister of justice had a great difficulty assembling personnel and filling in vacancies because there were few lawyers who were qualified to be judges and that was discussed at cabinet meetings. And then they would bring nominations to the Presidency to sign, and then these nominations were forwarded to the Assembly. So you have a whole set of appointments prior to the 11th of August signed by Karadzic that were published in the Official Gazette directly, only for some modifications to be later made by the Assembly because the MPs objected to certain people. Karadzic signed appointments for a large number of Croats and Muslims. And this met with resistance at the Assembly, so that eventually some of those people were revoked from those positions, including some Montenegrins even, because people at the local level objected to some people being judges there. Even Karadzic said it was very detrimental, very damaging, and Mr. Koljevic said the same. They said something along the lines: How are we supposed to build a democratic state if we act like this? You can read about this in one of the transcripts. I, however, did not decide on a single appointment. This was the proper procedure for appointments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What happened to those who belonged to the judiciary that was functioning before the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. They must have remained, most of them, even if some left. But I know that a -- they had a shortage of personnel because there were not enough lawyers, not enough qualified judges. And it was an even bigger problem when the Assembly refused to approve certain appointments and there was no replacement available or when a judge left of his own accord.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you raise your voice when the Assembly refused to approve certain appointments?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we did have a consultative meeting about these appointments and we were quite satisfied, because you cannot come across as a democratic state in the eyes of the international community if your own people are against judges simply because they belong to a different ethnic community. But the atmosphere was such that the MPs were convinced that it was up to them to decide. So when it came to a vote, they got their way. What I could do and what I did do as the speaker, I tried to organise discussions in such a way as to protect these nominations because it was politically wise and also fair in the humane sense. It was very politically unhelpful, to say the least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you point us to any of the stenographic notes or the minutes of the Assembly meetings where we can find confirmation of how you organised discussions in such a way as to protect these nominations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 11th of August there was a proposal for the MPs just to confirm an appointment signed by Mr. Karadzic, including a large number of Croats and Muslims. Prior to that, of course, I was in favour of approving these nominations. And there were deliberations and debate, and Karadzic himself defended his own proposal, Koljevic and others. You can find it in the record. As soon as it was placed on the agenda of the Assembly meeting, I took my position in favour of that proposal. 11th or 12th of August, one of those two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll check that overnight and see whether I can find that in the ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could bring it tomorrow, if you like, and we could see exactly who was appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At earlier occasions, were you aware of -- because I asked you before about -- about the fate of the judges that were functioning before the war. Was that ever discussed? You said: I don't know where they went, and you spoke then about new appointments.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, many of them were judges before. I really don't know what posts they occupied before, but they must have passed the bar exam. I don't know who served where, but I know about the Supreme Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a misunderstanding. I asked you whether it was ever discussed what happened with the judges who served before the war and may not have served anymore when the war had started.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was within the province of the minister, and I didn't get involved in that. I didn't find out why they did not occupy that post. Nobody actually wanted to be a judge during the war because anybody could take justice in their own hands at that time. They could barge into your courtroom and tell you what to do. That was within the province of the ministers I said. He is the one who formed the entire ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I earlier asked you whether you raised your voice in view of new nominations. Did you raise your voice when on the 25th of July, 1992, Mr. Lukic, who was the Vlasenica deputy to the Bosnian Serb Assembly, asked why we expelled all Muslim judges from Vlasenica, Bratunac, and Zvornik. Did you then comment on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who Lukic from Vlasenica is. Maybe Dukic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, I may have -- Rajko, yes, Rajko Lukic must be Rajko Dukic, yes. On the first name I --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. On the 25th of July I know that we were under great pressure to go as soon as possible to the London Conference. I even seem to recall that I didn't share all of that session, that Mr. Milanovic took over because we had to leave to make it to the London Conference. And that was our priority at that time. In that month, we went to London twice. I don't remember what happened there, and I do not trust myself to remember that now. There were all sorts of proposals and all sorts of speeches. What I cared about were the conclusions. Everybody else had the right to say whatever they pleased, and even if I objected it didn't matter one bit. All I could do was try to use my influence to arrive at a good decision at the end. If I objected, it could only lead discussion up a wrong path.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To go to more specific issue, also about the functioning of the judiciary, we heard the evidence of Mr. Mandic, who said he was very much in favour of the -- of the merging, I would say, of the military judicial organs with the -- with the civilian judicial organs. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And he told us that he discussed the matter with you. Is that also what your recollection tells you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have shown here that I put it before the Assembly, the military were against, and they took it off the agenda. However, it wasn't he who talked -- he talked with the government and then he talked to me. However, when the proposal from the government came, it was put before the Assembly. He understood that that was needed; however, the Main Staff was against and they managed to take it off the agenda. They did not accept the joinder. Health services were supposed to be joined, but the MPs rejected even that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said: They managed to get it off the agenda. On the basis of what exactly did they manage to get it off the agenda? I mean what was the competence of the military to remove items from the agenda of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the military did not have that right, but the so-called party concerned, the proponent was in this case the military prosecutor and they are under the Main Staff. And they come to the session to defend their position; the government defends its own position. They took opposite views, and after discussion the solomonious solution was found --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who proposed that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we arrived at it through debate. It was decided that was the best thing to do. I can't tell you now who decided that, but that solution was found to avoid making a decision then and there because the Main Staff was absolutely against and the government was backing a different proposal. Of course, it was possible to put it up for a vote, in which case one party would be out-voted and that would not have been a good thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I do understand that the government and the Main Staff had a different position. Who decided to postpone the matter? I mean, within whose competence was it to postpone the matter?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Assembly could agree with that or not. But the party's views have to be harmonised. Everybody has to substantiate their argument. We didn't want to play arbiters. We wanted them to bridge the gap between their positions. We didn't want to root for any of the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the "we" is not always clear to me, who "we" exactly was. Was the postponement to delay any further decision-making, was that put to a vote? If not, who then decided?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, if for instance you have a speaker chairing the Assembly session and one party is making a proposal, whereas another party is opposed. A debate follows. And if you are then placed in a situation to put something up for a vote without any hearing of arguments, then the only solution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, let me stop you at this moment. Let me then perhaps ask it directly, because it seems that -- did you decide that it would be postponed on the agenda? I mean, was it within the competence of you -- your --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no such power, but I could only approve the postponement. Of course I couldn't do it on my own, but I could propose -- I could suggest that it should be postponed, yes. And however, if the Assembly did not agree with that, my proposal would not pass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was there a vote on it or was it just silent decided -- you say: Let's postpone it and then without any further --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would never have put it on the agenda in the first place had I been against. Why would I have put it on the agenda then and then postponed it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find out who took that decision to postpone the matter. I now understand that it was you and you said -- let me just --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't take the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. You say: Of course, I couldn't do it on my own, but I could propose -- I could suggest that it should be postponed. And that's what you did, that it should be postponed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a long debate in which various interests clashed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did Mr. Mandic earlier or later address the same matter to the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember it. It was discussed by the government, by the Assembly, but we couldn't arrive at an agreed position. But it was not the problem that the prosecutor's office was separate from the judiciary. They could well work as separate institutions. Why not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mandic also testified that he specifically informed you about all matters in his knowledge, including irregularities and inhumane treatment in detention facilities. Could you confirm this or ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what he said. Later he said only as regards Sarajevo. But when Mr. Stewart was questioning me, I only informed him about Kula, because he wasn't aware of anything going on around Sarajevo. I know exactly what he said. And I know that he didn't know much more because otherwise he wouldn't have sent out that commission to investigate. You can find it in the transcript. You'll see that what I'm saying is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Krajisnik. Even for me I have to obey the laws of the clock. I have violated them too often. We'll adjourn for the day and we'll continue tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom.
